answers.reasoning: 'I heard a Negro play... the other night' marks the speaker as an observer recalling a recent performance.
'Pale dull pallor of an old gas light' creates a dim, worn setting matching the weary blues.
The 'poor piano moan[s] with melody'—the instrument seems to voice and share the sorrow.
'Rickety stool' is humble; 'like a musical fool' suggests abandon, total absorption in playing.
The exclamations 'O Blues!' 'Sweet Blues!' express the speaker's growing absorption and admiration.
Direct quotation in dialect lets the reader hear the musician's sorrow in his own voice and idiom.
'Thump, thump, thump' and 'played a few chords then he sang some more' mark a physical pause before the darker second song.
First song resolves to 'put ma troubles on the shelf'; second ends 'I wish that I had died'—resolve abandoned.
'Crooned' echoes 'mellow croon' of line 2, framing the night's performance.
'Temperate zone' contrasts with 'thrill of boyish agitation'; he thought himself past intense feeling, into emotional moderation.
Tender sense, nuptial verse, enjoyment—romantic investment in the marriage's meaning.
He 'pictured' her; the narrator frames his thought as idealization rather than observation; not explicitly declared false, nor medical.
He was drawn to her gayety because his life was gray from temperament—qualities he lacks.
Shift from his private feelings to what society said about her.
Ironic narratorial jab at society's certification of respectability.
Becoming like mourning crape on a rosy complexion—flattering costume.
'Ears shut' implies he deliberately ignores what is said about her.
'Passport to the set whose recognition she coveted' directly ties marriage to social ambition.
Hearth, pleasant room, good dinner establish settled domestic comfort framing his thrill of anticipation.
'Old trail of verse... floating through his enjoyment' shows half-remembered literary romance coloring his view of the marriage.
Her fondness for the child was what charmed him, suggesting attraction to tender domesticity; he had Lily brought to his house.
'Nothing was known of Mr. Haskett' so 'it was easy to believe the worst' — ignorance becomes license; verdict costs nothing.
'Took on an air of sanctity,' role of injured wife 'becoming to her as crape to a rosy complexion' — adapts public role to circumstances.
'True... Still' structure concedes propriety then shows persisting disapproval ('shook their heads', 'ears shut').

Clothes outgrown and frayed 'but for all that' something of the dandy, opal pin, carnation: elegance his circumstances can't quite support. Not indifference (neatly knotted), not wealth, not contrition (faculty note carnation not contrite).
'Rancor and aggrievedness' showing 'not a usual case'; real cause lay in manner and contempt, beyond listed offenses—personal resentment.
Introduced as illustration of what teachers couldn't put into words; the 'physical aversion' made concrete.
'Fell upon him without mercy, English teacher leading the pack' — pack of hunting animals attacking one quarry.
Smile never deserts him while fingers tremble: composure is performance masking strain.
'Usually attributed to insolence' after describing him as seeming to feel people watching him—narrator signals misreading of anxious watchfulness.
Passage filters Paul through teachers' hostility while physical details (trembling, glancing, 'hysterical') hint at fear they overlook. Other options overreach or contradict the text.
'Perplexity' means confusion; the father cannot understand his son. No evidence for siding, abandonment, or guilt over neglect.
'Suave and smiling' with a dandy's carnation contrasts with the contrite spirit expected of a suspended boy; polished composure at odds with situation.
'Peculiarly offensive in a boy' voices an adult/social norm that finds self-conscious theatrical display unfitting in a boy; not admiration, not medical, not Paul's embarrassment.
The simile suggests dilation like a drug's but the qualification 'which that drug does not produce' rules out that ordinary explanation, marking an unaccountable, unnatural intensity.
Lying as 'indispensable for overcoming friction' frames deception as a practical tool to smooth interactions; he is 'quite accustomed' to it.
Named offenses were disorder and impertinence, 'yet' the real cause lay in his hysterically defiant manner and undisguised contempt.
Three different classes, three forms of aversion/contempt, escalating from withdrawal (shading eyes, looking out window) to active mocking commentary.
Contrast: older boys cried, but Paul's set smile never deserted him, highlighting his unusual composure.
'Always glancing about him, seeming to feel that people might be watching him and trying to detect something' directly shows self-conscious performance under anxious scrutiny.

The 'old trail of verse' about nuptial door-posts is a literary, ceremonial allusion floating through his enjoyment; it idealizes marriage privately. No actual flowers, no worry, no recognition of trouble.
'Well-appointed' is usually applied to rooms/furnishings; here it conveys her polished, arranged composure. She has no deep anxiety (wastes no tissue in worry); no reluctance or official appointment.
The parenthetical question mimics society's vague, dismissive gossip about where Varick 'unearthed' her; free indirect style echoing condescension, not precision or Waythorn's plan.
The ironic 'easy to believe the worst' shows society judges on convenience and ignorance; narrator is detached, not endorsing; society accepted her promptly.
'This time' contrasts with the first divorce where Haskett, unknown, had no defenders. Not legal advocates, not Waythorn, and society did not turn firmly against her.
'Semi-widowhood' ironically grants a divorcee the sanctity and sympathy of a widow; Varick is alive. Narrator's tone is ironic, not sincere pity.
'Appear before the faculty' and 'account for his misdemeanors' use legal/judicial diction; the faculty state 'charges' against him, confirming a tribunal-like setting.
Paul enters 'suave and smiling' with a carnation the faculty feel is 'not properly significant of the contrite spirit' expected; suave marks polished composure clashing with expected penitence.
'Hysterical brilliancy,' 'theatrical,' 'peculiarly offensive,' and a 'glassy glitter' beyond what belladonna produces convey unnatural intensity, not innocence, actual addiction, or weak eyesight.
Lying is 'indispensable for overcoming friction'—a mechanical metaphor for smoothing over conflict with authority, as with the lie that he wants to return to school.
'Involuntary' and the 'shudder' show an instinctive recoil; the narrator links it to 'physical aversion,' not calculation; it is also 'unforgettable,' ruling out trivial.
Older boys wept under the 'baptism of fire,' but Paul's 'set smile did not once desert him'; the contrast emphasizes his rigid self-control, with only trembling fingers betraying discomfort.

'Droning' and 'drowsy' convey a heavy, languid sound; 'syncopated' adds an off-beat rhythmic quality. Nothing suggests the musician is asleep or that the speaker is bored; the speaker's mood is not set against the playing (which is 'lazy,' not lively).

Line 18: 'I heard that Negro sing, that old piano moan' places singing and moaning in grammatical parallel, fusing man and instrument into one lament. 'I heard' does not make the speaker join the song; 'old' and 'moan' options misread emphasis.

'Put ma troubles on the shelf' is a figurative expression for setting troubles aside temporarily; the next song ('can't be satisfied... wish that I had died') shows they are not overcome. Not literal, not triumph, not mockery.
